subject: council tax and the spare room

messages.text:
Hi Martin,

A quick one for the 2023-24 return before you file it. I do the freelance work from our spare room most evenings, roughly 30 hours a month last tax year. Can any of the council tax go against that? Hackney's bill for Albion Road was £1,845.32 for 2023/24, and Niamh and I split it.

Mei Lin (cc'd) is the friend I mentioned who has started doing some freelance data work. She asked me the same thing at book club so I said she could listen in. Hope that's ok.

Thanks,
Luis

Dear Luis,

Thank you for your email. There are two ways to claim for working from home as a sole trader, and you may use whichever gives the better result for the year.

The first is HMRC's simplified flat rate, which depends only on the hours you work at home. For 25 to 50 hours a month it is £10 a month, so £120 for a full year at 30 hours a month. No bills are needed, although you should be able to show roughly how many hours you worked.

The second is a proportion of your actual household costs, which can include council tax, electricity and gas (not rent in your case, as it would complicate matters for little benefit). The proportion is worked out by the number of rooms and by the share of time each room is used for business. Because you use the spare room for business only in the evenings, and only your half of the bill counts, the figure tends to come out very small.

My expectation is that the flat rate will be better for you, but if you send me the 2023/24 council tax bill I will check it properly before I file.

Mei Lin, I am happy for you to see this. The table attached applies to everyone, but I am afraid I cannot advise on your own position until we have an engagement letter in place.

Kind regards,
Martin Hale FCA
Hale Navarino Accountancy
3 Navarino Mews, London E8 | 020 7946 0921

- will email Martin separately about an engagement letter

Dear Luis,

Thank you, that is clear enough. On the actual-cost basis your half of the council tax, apportioned for one room of four and for 30 hours a month, comes to about £10 for the whole year. Adding gas and electricity would not bring it anywhere near £120, so you need not send those bills.

I've put £120 for use of home in the draft and noted the 30 hours a month. You should have the return to check by the end of the week.

Kind regards,
Martin Hale FCA

3 Navarino Mews, London E8 | 020 7946 0921

messages.text:
Hi Hamish,

A favour, and please say no if it's a bore. I've been asked to give a speech at the wedding in August, and it's the first one I've ever written in English for a room full of English people. I'm worried it reads like a translation. Could I send you the draft for your red pen? It's about a page.

Happy Easter. I'm halfway through the book, which is better than usual.

Luis

Dear Luis,

What marvellous news, and how like you to tuck it into the middle of a request for proofreading.  I had no idea that you and Niamh had decided, and I am delighted for you both.  Please give her my very warmest congratulations.

Of course I will read it.  Send it whenever you like.  I spent thirty-four years marking the prose of teenagers, and a groom's speech is a much kinder assignment, since its only real duty is to be short and to thank the right people in the right order.  I once sat through a groom who spoke for twenty-five minutes at a hotel in Peebles, and the cake began to lean.

I shall be in all weekend.  The garden needs me, but not urgently.

Yours,
Hamish Fairweather

Oh Hamish. It's not our wedding! It's my friends Aisha and Oliver's, on 16 August in the Cotswolds. I'm an usher, and Oliver has asked me to say a few words at the dinner the night before (Friday 15 August) because his brother can't do it. Niamh says she accepts the congratulations anyway.

The draft is below. The bits I'm least sure about are the opening and the line about the tent.

---

Good evening. For those who don't know me, I'm Luis, and I met Oliver in 2017 when we both turned up to the same flat viewing in Bermondsey and both lied about having a guarantor.

We didn't get the flat. But I got Oliver, who has since helped me move house twice, explained cricket to me four times, and once drove to Gatwick at 5am because I'd left my passport on his sofa.

Aisha, you will know by now that Oliver is a man who reads the instructions. All of them. He read the instructions for the tent you are going to sleep in on your honeymoon, and I believe he has opinions about them.

What I didn't know until I met you is that he also listens. To you, mainly. He talks about you the way other people talk about a city they've moved to and can't believe they live in.

So please raise your glasses to Aisha and Oliver, and to tomorrow.

---

Thanks for reading.

Luis

Dear Luis,

Please tell Niamh I am glad to have been of some use, even as comedy.  I withdraw my congratulations, but only provisionally.

As to the speech: it does not read like a translation.  It reads like a man who likes his friend, which is all anyone wants.  Three small things.

First, "both lied about having a guarantor" is your best line, and you should pause after it.  Let them laugh.

Second, the tent.  It is funny if the room knows about the tent and baffling if it does not.  If only six people know, cut it, and go straight from "reads the instructions" to the listening.  The contrast is better without the joke in between.

Third, "a city they've moved to and can't believe they live in" is lovely, and it is true of you, which is perhaps why it is so good.  Leave it exactly as it is.

It will take under three minutes.  Nobody's cake will lean.

Yours,
Hamish Fairweather

Thank you Hamish, this is perfect. The tent is gone (four people know about the tent). Pausing after the guarantor line.

Luis

truth.summary: Luis asked Hamish to read the toast he'll give at Aisha and Oliver's wedding dinner; Hamish thought it was Luis and Niamh's own wedding until Luis explained, then sent three notes, and Luis cut the tent joke.

subject: Pennywort Q1 plan (no need to read till you're back)

messages.text:
Hey Luis,

No reply needed, you're in Cork and should stay there. I was in the studio this morning to clear my desk and finished the Pennywort section of the Q1 planning doc while it was quiet, so it's there for when you're back. Steve still thinks they'll sign in the spring, so I've written it as the first three months from whenever we kick off, not as January to March.

I've left the catalogue and points history for later. Until we've watched people use the paper cards at the till, we're guessing what the tiers should be. Here's what I put down:

Month one: interviews in six of the Leeds and York shops with staff and regulars, plus a look at how the paper stamp cards are actually used at the till.
Month two: two or three tier structures on paper, tested with the same people.
Month three: one clickable prototype of sign-up and the points screen, no rewards catalogue yet.

I think Hannah will be all right with holding those two screens back if we show her what we found in the shops.

I've pencilled two days a week of Dev against it from month two and nothing from Gabi until month three.

For anything about the points API, ask Rhys; for the shop visits and travel budget, it's Sam's call, not mine.

Happy new year to you and Niamh.

Marcus

Marcus Adeyemi
Senior Product Designer, Acme Studio

messages.text:
Dear Luis,

As you know, the November meeting is at my house on Tuesday the 3rd, and I am, in the manner of all hosts who have not hosted for some years, already overthinking it.

I intend to make my almond sponge with three pears, which has been eaten without complaint since 1997.  But I have learnt that one must now ask about nuts, and I would not like to discover at a quarter past seven that someone cannot be in the same room as an almond.  I also need to know how many chairs to borrow from my neighbour, who lends them with a great deal of ceremony.

So would you be kind enough to let me know by Thursday 29 October whether you and Niamh will both be coming, and whether either of you has any difficulty with almonds?  I shall do the shopping on the Friday.

The door is the blue one with the unpruned rose.  The bell is unreliable, so knock as well, firmly.

I confess I have only reached page 212.  I suspect that I am not alone in this, and I shall pretend otherwise until somebody else confesses first.

Yours,
Hamish Fairweather
